title: Linux Home Server Setup
description: Learn how to install Linux on a home server, configure essential services like Nginx, UFW, and SSH, set up port forwarding, and configure dynamic DNS with No-IP.

pages.title: Installing Linux on Your Home Server
pages.why: A home server gives you full control over your data and services. Linux is the ideal operating system for servers because it is free, open-source, extremely stable, and has excellent support for networking and server software. Ubuntu Server is a popular choice because of its long-term support (LTS) releases, large community, and straightforward installation process.

instructions.text: Download the Ubuntu Server ISO from the official website (https://ubuntu.com/download/server). Choose the latest LTS version for stability.
Create a bootable USB drive using a tool like Balena Etcher, Rufus (Windows), or the dd command on Linux.
instructions.command: sudo dd if=ubuntu-24.04-live-server-amd64.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress
instructions.note: Replace /dev/sdX with your actual USB device. Be very careful to select the correct device — this will overwrite all data on it.

instructions.text: Insert the USB drive into your home server and boot from it. You may need to change the boot order in your BIOS/UEFI settings (usually accessed by pressing F2, F12, DEL, or ESC during boot).
Follow the Ubuntu Server installer. Choose your language, keyboard layout, and network configuration. For the disk setup, using the entire disk with LVM is recommended for flexibility.
Create your user account and set a strong password. Enable OpenSSH server when prompted — we will configure it further later.
After installation completes, remove the USB drive and reboot. Log in with the credentials you created.
Update the system to ensure all packages are current.
instructions.command: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

questions.text: Why is Linux preferred over Windows for a home server?
options: Linux has better gaming support
Linux is free, open-source, stable, and has excellent networking and server support
Linux comes pre-installed on most hardware
Linux does not require any updates

questions.text: What does the 'dd' command do when creating a bootable USB?
options: It downloads the ISO file from the internet
It formats the USB drive to NTFS
It copies the ISO image byte-by-byte to the USB device
It installs Linux directly onto the server

questions.text: Why is LVM recommended for disk setup?
options: It makes the disk faster
It provides flexibility to resize partitions and manage storage later
It encrypts the entire disk automatically
It is the only option that Ubuntu supports

pages.title: Installing and Configuring Nginx
pages.why: Nginx is a high-performance web server and reverse proxy. On your home server, it will serve web pages and can act as a gateway to other services you run. Nginx is known for its low memory footprint and ability to handle many concurrent connections, making it ideal for a home server with limited resources.

instructions.text: Install Nginx from the Ubuntu package repository.
Start the Nginx service and enable it to start automatically on boot.
instructions.command:
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx

instructions.text: Verify that Nginx is running.
instructions.note: You should see 'active (running)' in the output.

instructions.text: Test that Nginx is serving the default page by visiting your server's IP address in a web browser on the same network. You can find your server's IP with:
The default Nginx configuration file is located at /etc/nginx/sites-available/default. Review it to understand the basic structure.
To create your own site, create a new configuration file. For example:
instructions.note: A basic server block listens on port 80 and serves files from /var/www/mysite.

instructions.text: Enable the site by creating a symbolic link and test the configuration.
instructions.command:
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/mysite /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

questions.text: What is the primary role of Nginx on a home server?
options: It provides a firewall for your network
It serves web pages and acts as a reverse proxy
It manages user accounts on the system
It provides DNS resolution
It starts Nginx immediately
It installs Nginx from the repository
It configures Nginx to start automatically when the server boots
It opens port 80 in the firewall

questions.text: Why should you run 'nginx -t' before reloading the configuration?
options: To benchmark the server's performance
To test the configuration for syntax errors before applying it
To display the Nginx version
To list all active connections

pages.title: Setting Up UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall)
pages.why: A firewall is essential for securing your server. UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is a user-friendly front-end for iptables that makes it easy to manage firewall rules. Without a properly configured firewall, your server is exposed to every type of network attack. UFW lets you explicitly allow only the traffic you need, blocking everything else.

instructions.text: UFW is usually pre-installed on Ubuntu. Verify it is available.
instructions.note: If it shows 'inactive', that's expected — we haven't enabled it yet.

instructions.text: Before enabling UFW, allow SSH connections so you don't lock yourself out of the server.
Allow HTTP and HTTPS traffic for Nginx.
Enable UFW.
instructions.note: You will be asked to confirm. Type 'y' and press Enter. Make sure you have allowed SSH first!

instructions.text: Verify the firewall rules.
If you need to allow additional ports in the future, use the allow command.
instructions.note: This example allows TCP traffic on port 8080. Adjust as needed for your services.

instructions.text: To deny a specific port or remove a rule:
instructions.command:
sudo ufw deny 3306
sudo ufw delete allow 8080/tcp

questions.text: Why must you allow SSH before enabling UFW?
options: SSH is required for UFW to function
Without allowing SSH, you could lock yourself out of the server remotely
UFW does not start without SSH rules
SSH traffic is always blocked by default on Ubuntu

questions.text: What does 'Nginx Full' include when used with UFW?
options: Only port 80 (HTTP)
Only port 443 (HTTPS)
Both port 80 (HTTP) and port 443 (HTTPS)
Ports 80, 443, and 8080

questions.text: What is the default policy of UFW when enabled?
options: Allow all incoming and outgoing traffic
Deny all incoming traffic and allow all outgoing traffic
Block all traffic in both directions
Allow all incoming traffic and deny all outgoing traffic

pages.title: Configuring the SSH Daemon (sshd)
pages.why: SSH (Secure Shell) is the primary way you will remotely manage your server. Properly configuring sshd is critical for security. The default configuration works, but hardening it — disabling root login, changing the default port, and using key-based authentication — makes your server significantly more resistant to brute-force attacks and unauthorized access.

instructions.text: Verify that OpenSSH server is installed and running.
Open the SSH configuration file for editing.
Disable root login by finding the 'PermitRootLogin' line and setting it to 'no'.
instructions.note: This prevents anyone from logging in directly as root via SSH.

instructions.text: Optionally, change the default SSH port from 22 to a non-standard port (e.g. 2222) to reduce automated scanning.
instructions.note: If you change the port, remember to update your UFW rules and port forwarding accordingly.

instructions.text: Enable key-based authentication (it's usually enabled by default, but verify).
Generate an SSH key pair on your local machine (not the server) if you don't have one.
instructions.note: Press Enter to accept the default file location. Set a passphrase for extra security.

instructions.text: Copy your public key to the server.
Once key-based login works, disable password authentication for maximum security.
instructions.note: Only do this after confirming you can log in with your SSH key!

instructions.text: Restart the SSH service to apply changes.
If you changed the SSH port, update UFW.
instructions.command:
sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp
sudo ufw delete allow OpenSSH

questions.text: Why should you disable root login via SSH?
options: The root account does not exist on Ubuntu
To prevent direct remote access as root, reducing the risk of compromise
Because root cannot use SSH by design
To speed up SSH connections

questions.text: What is the advantage of key-based authentication over passwords?
options: Keys are shorter and easier to remember
Keys are immune to brute-force attacks and are significantly more secure
Keys don't require any configuration
Passwords are more secure but less convenient

questions.text: What should you do before disabling password authentication?
options: Disable the firewall
Reboot the server
Confirm that key-based authentication is working
Uninstall OpenSSH and reinstall it

pages.title: Setting Up Port Forwarding on Your Router
pages.why: Your home server sits behind your router, which uses NAT (Network Address Translation) to share one public IP address among all devices on your network. By default, incoming connections from the internet cannot reach your server. Port forwarding tells your router to direct traffic on specific ports to your server's internal IP address, making your services accessible from outside your local network.

instructions.text: Find your server's local IP address. This is the address you will forward traffic to.
instructions.note: Look for the address on your primary network interface (e.g. 192.168.1.x or 10.0.0.x). Ignore the 127.0.0.1 loopback address.

instructions.text: Consider assigning a static IP to your server so the address doesn't change. Edit the Netplan configuration:
instructions.note: Set a static address outside your router's DHCP range to avoid conflicts.

instructions.text: Apply the Netplan configuration.
Access your router's admin interface. This is usually at 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in your web browser. Log in with your router's admin credentials.
Navigate to the Port Forwarding section. This is often found under 'Advanced', 'NAT', or 'Firewall' settings depending on your router model.
Create port forwarding rules for the services you want to expose. Forward external port 80 (HTTP) to your server's internal IP on port 80, and external port 443 (HTTPS) to port 443.
If you changed your SSH port, forward that port as well (e.g. external port 2222 to internal port 2222).
instructions.note: Only forward SSH if you genuinely need remote access from outside your network. It increases your attack surface.

instructions.text: Save the router configuration and test from outside your network (e.g., using your mobile phone on cellular data) by navigating to your public IP address.
instructions.note: Run this on your server to find your public IP address.

questions.text: Why is port forwarding necessary to access your server from the internet?
options: Linux servers cannot connect to the internet without it
Your router uses NAT, so incoming traffic needs to be explicitly directed to your server's internal IP
Port forwarding encrypts the traffic for security
It increases your internet speed

questions.text: Why should you assign a static IP to your server?
options: Static IPs are faster than dynamic ones
So the port forwarding rules always point to the correct internal address
DHCP does not work with Linux servers
It is required by Nginx to function

questions.text: Should you forward your SSH port to the internet?
options: Always, it is required for the server to work
Never, SSH should be completely disabled
Only if you need remote access from outside your network, as it increases attack surface
Only on port 22, never on a custom port

pages.title: Setting Up Dynamic DNS with No-IP
pages.why: Most home internet connections have a dynamic IP address that changes periodically. This means the IP address you use to access your server from the internet may stop working after your ISP assigns you a new one. Dynamic DNS (DDNS) solves this by mapping a hostname (like myserver.ddns.net) to your current IP address and automatically updating it whenever it changes. No-IP is a popular free DDNS provider.

instructions.text: Create a free account at https://www.noip.com/. After registering, create a hostname (e.g. myserver.ddns.net) from the No-IP dashboard.
Install the No-IP Dynamic Update Client (DUC) on your server. First, download it.
instructions.command:
cd /usr/local/src
sudo wget https://www.noip.com/client/linux/noip-duc-linux.tar.gz
sudo tar xzf noip-duc-linux.tar.gz

instructions.text: Build and install the client.
instructions.command:
cd noip-2.1.9-1
sudo make
sudo make install
instructions.note: During installation, you'll be prompted for your No-IP email and password, and asked to choose which hostname to update.

instructions.text: Start the No-IP client.
Create a systemd service so the No-IP client starts automatically on boot. Create the service file:
Add the following content to the service file:
instructions.command:
[Unit]
Description=No-IP Dynamic DNS Update Client
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=forking
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/noip2
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

instructions.text: Enable and start the service.
instructions.command:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable noip2
sudo systemctl start noip2

instructions.text: Verify the service is running.
instructions.note: You should see 'active (running)'. The client will now automatically update your No-IP hostname with your current public IP.

instructions.text: Test your setup by accessing your server using your No-IP hostname from outside your network.
instructions.note: Replace myserver.ddns.net with your actual hostname. You should see the Nginx default page.

instructions.text: Optionally, update your Nginx server configuration to use your hostname.
instructions.note: Add this to your Nginx server block and reload Nginx.

questions.text: Why do you need Dynamic DNS for a home server?
options: To make your server faster
Because most home internet connections have a dynamic IP that changes, and DDNS keeps your hostname pointed at the current IP
To encrypt traffic between your server and the internet
Because DNS is required for Nginx to work

questions.text: What does the No-IP DUC (Dynamic Update Client) do?
options: It provides a firewall for your server
It monitors your public IP and updates the No-IP DNS record when it changes
It replaces your router's DNS settings
It assigns a static IP to your server

questions.text: Why should you create a systemd service for the No-IP client?
options: Systemd makes the client run faster
So the client starts automatically on boot and restarts if it crashes
Systemd is required for all Linux applications
To allow the client to modify firewall rules
